reasoning: ي is not a sun letter, so the article stays il-. Long uu and aa. Standard country name used in Palestinian speech.
Religious term that Palestinians really use (zakaat il-fiTr in Ramadan). The final ة after alif is said as a long aa when the word stands alone; it is zakaat only in a construct phrase.
Form II baTTal with a doubled emphatic ط, as in baTTal yidakhkhin 'he quit smoking'. The 'no longer' sense comes from baTTal + verb.
Taa marbuta after ج is e. In everyday use لهجة mainly means 'dialect', and 'accent' is the secondary sense.
Levantine colloquial uses nimir for tiger. In classical Arabic and the Gulf it tends to mean leopard. Vowels are short i, i.

Fixed religious condolence formula that is genuinely said at Palestinian funerals, with the plural ending -kum. The doubled ظ is written THTH. The more colloquial alternative is il-ba'iyye bi-7ayaatkum.
Passive participle of Form X, commonly said for used or secondhand goods such as a car. Some speakers say mista3mal.
شو is shu, and the present-tense bti- prefix marks the 2nd person m. The verb ishtaghal is usually said with a reduced vowel in the imperfect (btishtghil). Literally 'what do you work?'.
Palestinian 7ilu has a short i and final u. In daily speech it most often means pretty, nice or cute, and 'sweet' is only the taste sense.
bi- prefix plus kfii plus -ni, 'it is enough for me'. The long ii comes from the verb kafa/yikfi.
ع plus il- contracts to 3al-. il-balad means the town centre or downtown. law sama7t is the normal polite 'please' to a m. sg.
MSA-origin word that Palestinians use normally. Taa marbuta after م is e.
The pattern CiCaaCa drops the first short vowel in Palestinian, like ktaab, so zbaale. Taa marbuta after ل is e. Some speakers say zibaale.
wa3ad plus -ni, with the colloquial inno 'that' in place of MSA anna.
khalli plus -ni followed by a subjunctive verb. The 'and' is said u before the b- of barja3lak, 'I'll come back to you'. The -lak ending addresses a m. sg.

vowelled_arabic: اللِّي عَلَى رَاسُو بَطْحَة بِيِحَسِّس عَلِيهَا
reasoning: Well-known Palestinian proverb. اللي is illi, raaso has the -o suffix, and 3aleeha has ee. Taa marbuta after ح is said a. The 3rd-person prefix might be contracted to bi7assis in fast speech.
Palestinian 'who' is miin with a long ii, not MSA man.
ث is said t in Palestinian, so ثاني is taani. ع plus il- before the sun letter ش gives 3ash-shimaal. Standard phrase for giving directions.

As written, ending in ى, this is the past 'he let'. The imperative 'let things go' would be khalli, and the context may intend that. The article loses its i after the vowel-final verb, and the hamza is kept after the article.
Everyday word, so ق is a glottal stop. The 1st person vowelling is uncertain: it could be zihi't, zhi't or zaha't. Literally 'I got bored/fed up'.
Country name with a short u and a long aa.

3een becomes 3eeno with the -o suffix. The f. participle loses its short vowel: waasi3a becomes waas3a. The idiom is understood as 'greedy/covetous', though 3eeno faarghe is the more typical wording for greedy.
rii7a plus -o gives rii7to. zaakye is the f. of zaaki, meaning tasty or fragrant. The hamza of الأكل is written after the article.
ما negates the verb, and the past of 'go' is ru7t with a short u. li'inno 'because' follows the spelling, and la'inno is a common variant.
Literally 'he opened his eye'. The figurative sense is that he woke up to reality. The emphatic form fatta7 3eeno 'be alert' is also common.
